title: Covariance Geometry of Basis-Resolved Low-Energy Wavefunctions in the Spin-$1/2$ Kitaev--Heisenberg Model
authors: Sk Saniur Rahaman, S. R. Hassan
abstract: We develop a basis-resolved covariance framework for investigating the organization of low-energy many-body wavefunctions in the spin-$1/2$ Kitaev--Heisenberg model. By constructing covariance matrices from local-spin, bond-correlation, and plaquette-flux representations of the low-energy states, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is employed to identify the dominant collective covariance modes. We find a systematic evolution of the covariance geometry across the phase diagram: magnetically ordered phases are described by an essentially one-dimensional covariance manifold, conventional magnetic phase boundaries exhibit competition between leading covariance modes, whereas the Kitaev regimes develop intrinsically multidimensional covariance geometry. Furthermore, the same many-body wavefunction produces distinct covariance geometries in different operator representations, demonstrating that covariance geometry is determined jointly by the quantum state and the physical observables used to probe it. Shannon entropy and the participation ratio provide quantitative measures of this evolution. The present framework establishes basis-resolved covariance geometry as a complementary statistical perspective for characterizing frustrated quantum many-body systems beyond conventional order parameters.
summary: This work introduces a novel basis-resolved covariance framework to statistically characterize low-energy wavefunctions in the Kitaev–Heisenberg model. By analyzing how local spin, bond correlations, and plaquette fluxes co-vary across the phase diagram using PCA, the authors map out the quantum state's statistical geometry. This reveals that the complexity of the wavefunction structure changes fundamentally when moving into exotic Kitaev spin liquid regimes.
main_problem: The study aims to characterize the organization of low-energy many-body wavefunctions in strongly correlated quantum systems, particularly where conventional order parameters fail.
main_result: The covariance geometry varies significantly across the phase diagram: ordered phases are 1D, Kitaev regimes show intrinsic multidimensionality, and this geometry depends on the physical observable used for probing.
method: A basis-resolved covariance framework is developed using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) applied to feature vectors derived from local-spin, bond-correlation, and plaquette-flux operators.
model_or_system: The system studied is the spin-$1/2$ Kitaev–Heisenberg model on a honeycomb lattice. The Hamiltonian interpolates between Heisenberg and Kitaev limits via coupling parameters J and K.
key_observables: Covariance geometry (quantified by Shannon entropy and Participation Ratio), principal covariance modes, local-spin expectation values, bond correlations, and plaquette fluxes.
important_parameters: The interaction parameter $\phi$, which tunes the system across various quantum phases including magnetically ordered states and Kitaev spin liquid regimes.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that constructing feature vectors from specific physical operators (local-spin, bond, flux) provides a statistically meaningful representation of the wavefunction's structure for PCA.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the honeycomb lattice structure and show covariance spectra/principal components across different phases; Tables summarize Shannon entropy and Participation Ratio values for various representations.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the framework by defining basis-resolved feature spaces using multiple physical operators, calculates the ensemble covariance matrix over the phase diagram, and analyzes its statistical geometry using PCA, entropy, and participation ratio to map out phase transitions statistically.
why_interesting: While focused on magnetism, the use of advanced statistical tools like covariance geometry provides a generalizable method for characterizing complex quantum states beyond simple symmetry breaking, which is relevant across many-body physics.

The elementary plaquettes,P1, . . . , P8, are labeled for constructing the plaquette-flux operators used in the covariance analysis.

FIG. 2. Ground-state and first-excited-state energies per site for the N = 16 Kitaev–Heisenberg model obtained using the SALE–SD method (solid lines) and exact diagonaliza- tion (dashed lines) as functions of the interaction parame- ter ϕ. The excellent agreement demonstrates that the re- duced symmetry-adapted basis accurately reproduces the low- energy spectrum throughout the phase diagram.

FIG. 3. Expansion coefficients of the ground state (GS) and first excited state (FES) for representative interaction parameters across the Kitaev–Heisenberg phase diagram. For each state, the upper panel shows the coefficient magnitudes |Ck| arranged in decreasing order, while the lower panel displays the signs of the first 200 coefficients. Only these leading signs are displayed clearly, since the signs of all 1000 retained coefficients become visually unresolved when plotted together. The covariance analysis nevertheless uses all M = 1000 retained basis configurations.

Panels (a)–(c) correspond to the ground state, while panels (d)–(f) show the corresponding results for the first excited state. For each observable, row (i) presents the normalized covariance eigenvalues λα, row (ii) the corresponding covariance eigenvectors wα, and row (iii) the quantified principal components Qα(ϕ) defined in Eq. The evolution of these ingredients across ordered phases, magnetic phase boundaries, and Kitaev regimes provides the microscopic foundation for the changes in covariance geometry discussed below.
